name: New Algorithms Needed
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Algorithm Gap: Better Hardware Alone Does Not Buy You Anything Useful
lesson.summary: The list of quantum algorithms with a proven, meaningful advantage over the best classical alternatives is still short, and building better hardware does not by itself create new reasons to use it.
lesson.body:
It is easy to assume that once quantum hardware gets good enough, useful applications will simply follow. That assumption skips over a separate, harder problem: even a perfect, error-free quantum computer is only as valuable as the algorithms that know how to use it. Recall the narrow problem applicability of quantum computing covered earlier in this course. Today's list of quantum algorithms with a rigorously proven advantage over the best known classical approach is genuinely short: Shor's algorithm for factoring large numbers, Grover's algorithm for unstructured search, and simulating certain quantum mechanical systems that are themselves hard to model classically. That is close to the entire proven list.

Even within that short list, the size of the advantage varies enormously, and this is where a lot of public excitement gets ahead of the math. Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speedup, meaning a search that takes a classical computer roughly N steps takes a quantum computer roughly the square root of N steps. That sounds impressive until you plug in real numbers. For a problem where N is one trillion, a classical computer needs about one trillion steps, while Grover's algorithm needs about one million, a real and meaningful reduction. But each of those million quantum steps has to be executed with extremely low error, using hardware that is dramatically more expensive and harder to build than classical hardware. Once you account for the overhead of error correction covered elsewhere in this course, a quadratic speedup can be far less decisive in practice than it looks in a textbook, and for many real problems classical hardware improving steadily every year can simply outrun a quantum algorithm with only a quadratic edge.

Beyond the proven cases, there is a large body of proposed quantum algorithms, particularly optimization heuristics used for chemistry, materials, and logistics problems, whose actual advantage over the best classical heuristics is unproven and, in a number of documented cases, has shrunk or disappeared entirely once classical researchers looked harder at the comparison. This is not a hardware problem at all, it is an open question in mathematics and theoretical computer science: does a genuinely useful quantum algorithm exist for a given real-world problem, and if so, has anyone found it yet.

This is why "new algorithms needed" belongs on the list of required breakthroughs alongside hardware improvements. A faster, cheaper, better-connected quantum computer running only today's known algorithms would still only be useful for a narrow slice of problems. Closing that gap requires discovery, not just engineering, and discovery does not arrive on a predictable schedule just because more funding or more qubits become available.
